profile.campus: The Dalles, Wasco County, Oregon (Google's original self-built data center campus)
profile.address: West 2nd Street, The Dalles, Wasco County, Oregon, 97058
profile.reading: This building is the second of two data center structures Google has built along West 2nd Street on its original Dalles campus, the site where Google began constructing its first self-operated data center in 2006, marking the start of Google building and operating its own data center infrastructure rather than leasing it from third parties. Google's own data center locations page lists Oregon among its earliest and most significant US data center states, and the company has stated it has invested more than $7 billion in Oregon infrastructure since 2006, spread across the multiple buildings that now make up the Dalles campus. Google began construction of a fourth building at the site in 2015, expanding beyond the original two-building footprint reflected in OpenStreetMap's mapping of this location. Google chose The Dalles for its location along the Columbia River, which provided both hydroelectric power access from Bonneville Power Administration dams and river water Google has used for cooling, a choice that later became the subject of a long-running local dispute. Fortune's longform reporting and Oregon Public Broadcasting have both covered tension between Google and the City of The Dalles over how much of the city's water rights the data center campus consumes for cooling, with some residents quoted describing the company's local reputation shifting over nearly two decades of expansion. The Dalles campus predates Google's newer Taylor Lake data center project nearby, and this registry treats the original West 2nd Street buildings and the Taylor Lake buildings as distinct facilities despite sharing the same Wasco County campus and operator. Google has not disclosed which specific building on West 2nd Street this OSM-mapped structure corresponds to, nor its individual power capacity or floor area, consistent with Google's general practice of reporting investment and jobs figures only at the state or metro level rather than per building. This registry records the state-level $7 billion Oregon investment figure as regional context rather than attributing it to any single building, and flags county assessor parcel records as the next real research step for building-specific square footage.

sources.title: Oregon Public Broadcasting coverage of Google Dalles water use

profile.capacity_note: not published at individual building level
profile.facility_note: Part of Google's original West 2nd Street data center campus in The Dalles, one of two similarly unlabeled buildings OpenStreetMap contributors have mapped at this location.

profile.regional_context: Oregon has no state sales tax, and Wasco County's enterprise zone program has abated local property taxes on Google's Dalles investment for years at a time under agreements renewed as each new building comes online, a structure local officials credit with anchoring Google's continued expansion at the site since 2006.

reading.body:
Google does not publish the individual megawatt capacity, square footage, or building count of its Dalles, Wasco County campus, though the company confirmed ownership of this facility on September 3, 2026. The site is part of a single contiguous data center campus that Google began building in 2006 as its first internally operated facility, then expanded with a fourth building from 2015 onward. Google reports cumulative investment of more than $7 billion in Oregon since 2006, citing energy infrastructure, workforce, and policy as reasons for the choice.

Without published capacity for this individual campus, its scale cannot be directly compared to other facilities. Oregon as a state has 133 mapped data center locations but only 8 publish megawatt figures; those eight total 156.6 MW. This Dalles campus ranks 9th among Oregon facilities by the state's own published figures, a ranking that reflects only the subset of operators disclosing numbers, not the actual capacity hierarchy. The inability to measure this facility against state and national AI infrastructure makes it impossible to assess whether it remains, as historical reporting suggested, a single most significant Google site or how much of Google's Oregon buildout it represents.

Whether this campus matters to AI scaling depends on facts Google has not published. The company's opacity on individual facility capacity obscures the grid constraint question this analysis requires: how much compute lives here, when was it added, and whether Oregon's energy infrastructure can sustain planned expansion. Local reporting has documented water use tensions between Google and the City of The Dalles, a potential infrastructure limit not captured in power specifications. The gap between historical prominence and current invisibility in published data suggests the site remains substantial, but its role in AI scaling cannot be read from disclosed facts.
